input.said: What does Seth use the Antikythera mechanism to show?

cases.reply:
He uses it as an example that computers don't have to be digital Turing machines. The earliest computers, he says, were analogue devices that worked in continuous time, and the Antikythera mechanism is his "excellent example" [spya-zg9me8]. The point sits in the "Other games in town" section. There he argues that Turing-style algorithms (step-by-step rules that turn one string of symbols into another) are only one kind of computation. Biological systems are full of continuous and random dynamics, so it is "presumptuous" to assume only Turing computation matters for consciousness [spya-n393ru]. The example is a short historical aside. It supports his claim that broader kinds of computation exist and are more tied to their physical material than digital computing is [spya-gamzr3 spya-kjfjgm].

The article gives the date as "around 2,000 BCE" [spya-zg9me8]. That looks like a slip. [World History Encyclopedia](https://www.worldhistory.org/Antikythera_Mechanism/) dates the device to roughly 205–60 BCE, and [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antikythera_mechanism) says it was made in the 2nd century BC. "About 2,000 years ago" is probably what was meant. This doesn't affect his argument.

input.said: What does Seth say about Chalmers' neural replacement thought experiment?

cases.reply:
Seth says the thought experiment fails at the start, because its central premise can't be met. The experiment asks us to imagine swapping brain parts one by one for silicon parts that behave identically, and concludes that consciousness must be substrate independent. Seth calls it a popular trope, mentions that Hinton used it to claim conscious AI is already here, and says it "fails at its first hurdle" because a perfect silicon replacement for any part of the brain is impossible [spya-ahtr6e].

His reasoning comes just before that. Real brains are tightly integrated across scales, which he links to "generative entrenchment." So you can't assume a single neuron can be swapped for a silicon equivalent that keeps its input-output behavior exactly the same [spya-jnwfxp]. His example is work by Chintaluri and Vogels, who found that some neurons fire spikes apparently to clear metabolic waste. Replacing those neurons would mean building a silicon metabolism too, and he says silicon isn't suited to that [spya-un9fjn].

In the argument as a whole, this is a consequence of his first claim, that brains are not computers, which he builds around the missing split between "what they do" and "what they are" [spya-zw2m7u]. The thought experiment needs that split, which is why he uses the point against it.

The article doesn't say how Chalmers or others would answer. My inference is that a defender could treat the experiment as an idealization, which would shift the dispute to whether the replacement is possible in principle. Seth's text only argues it is impossible in practice.

input.said: What does he say McCulloch and Pitts showed?

cases.reply:
He says McCulloch and Pitts showed, in a landmark paper, that networks of highly simplified abstract neurons can perform logical operations. The "Turing complete" part came later, and he credits it to Kleene and others, not to McCulloch and Pitts. Given a tape-like memory, as in the Turing machine, such networks could in principle implement any algorithm.

The Figure 2 caption describes the original neuron. It summed weighted inputs and gave an output of 1 if the sum passed a fixed threshold, and 0 if it didn't.

In the argument, this result is one half of what he calls a "mathematical marriage of convenience". It lets you ignore the messy neurobiological reality of real brains and still get everything Turing computation offers. He sets it up so that the next paragraphs can attack it. He says today's artificial neural networks are direct descendants of McCulloch, Pitts and Kleene. He then argues that real brains have no sharp separation between "mindware" and "wetware".
